name: Authentication & Passwords
description: Password security, biometrics, multi-factor and passwordless authentication (FIDO/WebAuthn).

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers here, all from USENIX 2018, treat passwords as a stubborn fact of life and try to understand or patch their weaknesses rather than replace them. Several are empirical and human-centered: "Better managed than memorized? Studying the Impact of Managers on Password Strength and Reuse" (2018) and "Forgetting of Passwords: Ecological Theory and Data" (2018) probe how real users cope with memory and tooling, while "The Rewards and Costs of Stronger Passwords in a University" (2018) studies how an actual password policy plays out at scale. Alongside these sit early systems and protocol concerns — "Rethinking Access Control and Authentication for the Home Internet of Things (IoT)" (2018) reframes authentication for multi-user device settings, and "O Single Sign-Off, Where Art Thou?" (2018) exposes session and account-hijacking gaps in SSO. This year sets the tone: passwords are insecure but entrenched, so the work is about measuring damage and hardening the ecosystem.

By 2019-2020 the field pivots from individual passwords toward the broader account-protection ecosystem and toward biometrics as an alternative. "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting" (USENIX 2019) operationalizes breach data to defend accounts at scale, and "Birthday, Name and Bifacial-security" (2019) broadens the empirical lens beyond English-speaking users to Chinese passwords. At the same time, biometrics and liveness become central: "Void: A fast and light voice liveness detection system" (USENIX 2020) and "Liveness is Not Enough: Enhancing Fingerprint Authentication with Behavioral Biometrics to Defeat Puppet Attacks" (2020) show both the promise and the spoofing risks of biometric factors. Two-factor authentication also arrives as a serious object of study with "Empirical Measurement of Systemic 2FA Usability" (2020), shifting attention from whether 2FA is secure to whether organizations can actually live with it.

From 2021 to 2022 the work increasingly targets adoption, deployment, and the fragility of newer factors. "Driving 2FA Adoption at Scale" (USENIX 2021) turns 2FA into a design and behavioral problem of nudging users, while "Inexpensive Brainwave Authentication" (2021) and "Card Brand Mixup Attack" (2021) explore exotic biometrics and break real payment-card authentication respectively. Deepfakes raise the stakes for biometric trust in "Seeing is Living? Rethinking the Security of Facial Liveness Verification in the Deepfake Era" (USENIX 2022), and email-authentication measurement matures with "A Large-scale and Longitudinal Measurement Study of DKIM Deployment" (2022).

Most recently, USENIX 2023 shows two clear fronts. On classic passwords, machine learning sharpens guessing attacks and evaluation — "Improving Real-world Password Guessing Attacks via Bi-directional Transformers" (2023), "Password Guessing Using Random Forest" (2023), and "Pass2Edit" (2023) model how users create and edit passwords, while "No Single Silver Bullet: Measuring the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters" (2023) audits the meters meant to guide users. On the ecosystem side, "A Study of Multi-Factor and Risk-Based Authentication Availability" (2023) measures how far real services have actually moved beyond plain passwords, and emerging interfaces draw scrutiny in "Hidden Reality: Caution, Your Hand Gesture Inputs in the Immersive Virtual World are Visible to All!" (2023). The arc runs from measuring password pain, to building account-protection and biometric defenses, to ML-driven attack/defense and broad measurement of whether multi-factor and risk-based authentication are reaching users.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this NDSS slice, around 2018, splits cleanly between shoring up passwords and finding something better than them. On the password side, "A Security Analysis of Honeywords" (NDSS 2018) scrutinized the decoy-password idea meant to detect database breaches, while a wave of biometric papers looked for alternatives: "Face Flashing: a Secure Liveness Detection Protocol based on Light Reflections" and "rtCaptcha: A Real-Time CAPTCHA Based Liveness Detection System" (both NDSS 2018) attacked the core problem of telling a live human from a replayed photo or video, and "K-means++ vs. Behavioral Biometrics" (NDSS 2018) probed how sound behavioral-biometric authentication really was. Even at this stage the community was as interested in breaking these systems as building them — "Broken Fingers: On the Usage of the Fingerprint API in Android" (NDSS 2018) showed developers routinely misused the platform's own fingerprint API.

The next few years pushed on measurement, deployed protocols, and new sensing modalities. "Distinguishing Attacks from Legitimate Authentication Traffic at Scale" (NDSS 2019) tackled online password-guessing defenses without locking out real users, and "Robust Performance Metrics for Authentication Systems" (NDSS 2019) argued the field was measuring ML-based authenticators wrong in the first place. A striking shift was authentication moving onto the body and into new hardware: "OcuLock: Exploring Human Visual System for Authentication in Virtual Reality Head-mounted Display" (NDSS 2020) opened VR eye-based auth, while "On the Resilience of Biometric Authentication Systems against Random Inputs" (NDSS 2020) kept the adversarial pressure on. The passwordless future also got formal scrutiny with "A Formal Analysis of the FIDO UAF Protocol" (NDSS 2021), even as "On the Insecurity of SMS One-Time Password Messages" (NDSS 2021) documented how weak the still-dominant second factor really was.

By the mid-2020s two threads dominate: increasingly creative side-channel attacks on biometrics, and authentication spreading across devices and ecosystems. "PrintListener: Uncovering the Vulnerability of Fingerprint Authentication via the Finger Friction Sound" (NDSS 2024) and "EMIRIS: Eavesdropping on Iris Information via Electromagnetic Side Channel" (NDSS 2025) showed that fingerprints and irises leak through channels their designers never anticipated, while "UniID: Spoofing Face Authentication System by Universal Identity" (NDSS 2024) and "Maginot Line" (NDSS 2024) exposed weaknesses in face auth and PII-as-a-factor logins. Behavioral and continuous approaches matured too, from "AuthentiSense" few-shot mobile biometrics (NDSS 2023) toward always-on schemes.

The most recent work (NDSS 2026) shows the field has not converged on any single answer — passwords, tokens, biometrics, and cross-device flows all remain live problems. Password guessing is very much alive, with "Targeted Password Guessing Using k-Nearest Neighbors" and "CoT-DPG: A Co-Training based Dynamic Password Guessing Method" both advancing attacker models, while "Vault Raider: Stealthy UI-based Attacks Against Password Managers in Desktop Environments" targets the tools meant to save us from passwords. Token-based access drew fresh scrutiny in "Token Time Bomb: Evaluating JWT Implementations" and "NetCap: Data-Plane Capability-Based Defense Against Token Theft." Meanwhile the frontier pushes toward frictionless, continuous, and cross-device authentication — "Know Me by My Pulse: Toward Practical Continuous Authentication on Wearable Devices via Wrist-Worn PPG" and "Anchors of Trust: A Usability Study on User Awareness, Consent, and Control in Cross-Device Authentication" — signaling that usability and continuous verification, not just one-time login, are where the area now stands.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treats authentication as a usability-and-economics problem layered on top of passwords and second factors. At IEEE S&P 2018, "A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability" measured whether hardware second factors were actually deployable by ordinary users, while "On the Economics of Offline Password Cracking" reframed password strength as a quantitative adversarial cost model rather than a heuristic. Alongside these, "When Your Fitness Tracker Betrays You" (S&P 2018) and "Do You Feel What I Hear?" (S&P 2018) opened two threads that recur throughout the decade: behavioral biometrics as both an authenticator and a leakage channel, and sensor-context pairing for devices without keyboards.

The 2019-2021 period is dominated by machine learning cutting both ways on passwords. "Beyond Credential Stuffing: Password Similarity Models Using Neural Networks" (S&P 2019) showed attackers could exploit how users mutate one password across sites, and "Improving Password Guessing via Representation Learning" (S&P 2021) pushed learned generative guessing further, while "Reasoning Analytically about Password-Cracking Software" (S&P 2019) worked to make strength estimates principled. In parallel the field began seriously testing password replacements: "Is FIDO2 the Kingslayer of User Authentication?" (S&P 2020) ran a comparative usability study of passwordless FIDO2, "True2F" (S&P 2019) hardened second-factor tokens against backdoors, and biometric authenticators came under attack in "Who is Real Bob? Adversarial Attacks on Speaker Recognition Systems" (S&P 2021). Empirical human-factors work such as "This PIN Can Be Easily Guessed" (S&P 2020) kept grounding the theory in what people actually choose.

By 2022-2023 the emphasis shifts from asking whether to move past passwords to formally proving the replacements are sound and probing their new attack surfaces. "FIDO2, CTAP 2.1, and WebAuthn 2: Provable Security and Post-Quantum Instantiation" (S&P 2023) and "Token meets Wallet: Formalizing Privacy and Revocation for FIDO2" (S&P 2023) gave the passwordless standard rigorous foundations, while "MPCAuth" (S&P 2023) and "zk-creds" (S&P 2023) rebuilt multi-factor and anonymous credentials on distributed-trust and zero-knowledge primitives. New modalities and their weaknesses appear together: "SoK: Authentication in Augmented and Virtual Reality" (S&P 2022) mapped the AR/VR space that "Low-effort VR Headset User Authentication Using Head-reverberated Sounds" (S&P 2023) then built into, and "Breaking Security-Critical Voice Authentication" (S&P 2023) showed voice biometrics remained fragile. Honeywords ("How to Attack and Generate Honeywords," S&P 2022) and EMV payment authentication ("The EMV Standard: Break, Fix, Verify," S&P 2021; "Practical EMV Relay Protection," S&P 2022) round out a period focused on breaking and formally fixing deployed systems.

The most recent work, clustered at S&P 2026, reflects a field where passkeys are arriving in the real world and large language models have entered both attack and defense. "The Passkey Promise: A Comparative Usability Study of MFA Methods" (S&P 2026) revisits the FIDO2 usability question now that passkeys are mainstream, echoing the 2020 Kingslayer study a full generation later. Password guessing has consolidated around learned models with efforts to standardize and improve them, seen in "MAYA: Addressing Inconsistencies in Generative Password Guessing Through a Unified Benchmark" (S&P 2026) and "MoPE: A Mixture of Password Experts" (S&P 2026), while "Can Foundation LLMs Accurately Estimate Password Strength and Provide Appropriate Password Feedback?" (S&P 2026) tests whether general-purpose LLMs can replace bespoke strength meters. At the same time the attack surface has moved up the stack to federated identity and pairing ecosystems, with "Demystifying the (In)Security of OAuth-Based Account Linking in Connector Ecosystems," "C-Verifier" on AWS Cognito, and "One Tap to Hijack Them All" on Google Fast Pair (all S&P 2026), and sensing-based biometrics continue with "2FiA: Towards WiFi Sensing-Based Authentication with Unique Biometrics" (S&P 2026). The arc runs from making passwords survivable, to replacing and formally proving them, to securing the sprawling identity and pairing infrastructure that passwordless authentication now depends on.

ccs.narrative:
Authentication research at CCS has covered the full lifecycle of credential security, from password strength estimation to biometric modalities and passwordless standards. On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters (CCS 2018) revealed that deployed meters systematically misestimate real-world password strength, undermining user guidance at scale. A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication (CCS 2018) contributed on the protocol side, formally verifying the 5G AKA handshake. CAPTCHA-breaking received renewed attention with Yet Another Text Captcha Solver: A Generative Adversarial Network Based Approach (CCS 2018), which demonstrated GAN-based solvers require only small training sets.

Compromised credential management became practical in 2019: Protocols for Checking Compromised Credentials (CCS 2019) designed privacy-preserving protocols enabling users to check breached credentials without exposing them to the checking service. Domain Validation++ For MitM-Resilient PKI (CCS 2018) strengthened certificate issuance against network-level adversaries.

Beyond passwords, sensor-based authentication expanded. PatternListener: Cracking Android Pattern Lock Using Acoustic Signals (CCS 2018) cracked gesture-based locks acoustically, DeMiCPU: Device Fingerprinting with Magnetic Signals Radiated by CPU (CCS 2019) fingerprinted hardware using magnetic emissions, and EchoHand: High Accuracy and Presentation Attack Resistant Hand Authentication on Commodity Mobile Devices (CCS 2022) used acoustic hand geometry for biometric authentication with strong liveness guarantees.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this set, from 2018, is dominated by two concerns: making passwords measurably better and figuring out whether the alternatives are usable. On the password side, "On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters" (CCS 2018) questioned whether the meters users see every day actually track real guessability, while "On the Economics of Offline Password Cracking" (S&P 2018) reframed strength as an economic contest between defenders and crackers, and "A Security Analysis of Honeywords" (NDSS 2018) scrutinized decoy-password schemes meant to detect breaches. In parallel, "A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability" (S&P 2018) put hardware two-factor tokens under a human-factors microscope, foreshadowing the field's lasting split between raw security and whether people will actually adopt it. A vein of biometric and liveness work also opens here, with "Face Flashing" (NDSS 2018) defending face authentication against spoofing.

Around 2019-2020 the center of gravity shifts to breached credentials and machine learning. As password dumps piled up, the community moved from "pick a strong password" to "assume it already leaked": "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting" (USENIX 2019) and "Protocols for Checking Compromised Credentials" (CCS 2019) built privacy-preserving ways to check a password against known breaches, while "Beyond Credential Stuffing: Password Similarity Models Using Neural Networks" (S&P 2019) and later "Improving Password Guessing via Representation Learning" (S&P 2021) showed neural nets could model how humans mangle and reuse passwords. The same period marks the real arrival of the passwordless future: "Is FIDO2 the Kingslayer of User Authentication?" (S&P 2020) gave the FIDO2/WebAuthn standard its first serious comparative usability study, testing whether hardware-backed public-key login could finally displace the password.

As authentication spread onto phones, voice assistants, and headsets, so did the attack surface for biometrics. "Liveness is Not Enough" (USENIX 2020) and "Void" (USENIX 2020) hardened fingerprint and voice liveness detection, "Who is Real Bob? Adversarial Attacks on Speaker Recognition Systems" (S&P 2021) showed speaker-recognition biometrics were vulnerable to adversarial audio, and a new AR/VR thread emerged with "OcuLock" (NDSS 2020) using the human visual system to authenticate in VR headsets and "SoK: Authentication in Augmented and Virtual Reality" (S&P 2022) mapping out that space. Identity itself also became a research object, with "CanDID" (S&P 2021) and "zk-creds" (S&P 2023) building decentralized, privacy-preserving credentials on zero-knowledge proofs.

The most recent work, the 2026 NDSS batch, shows the area maturing along every one of these fronts at once. Password guessing keeps advancing with "Targeted Password Guessing Using k-Nearest Neighbors" and "CoT-DPG: A Co-Training based Dynamic Password Guessing Method," while the attack surface has moved to the plumbing of modern login: "Vault Raider" attacks password managers through the desktop UI, "Token Time Bomb" audits JWT implementations, and "NetCap" defends access tokens against theft. Device pairing and its formal underpinnings return with "BLERP: BLE Re-Pairing Attacks and Defenses" and "Formal Analysis of BLE Secure Connection Pairing," and the usability lens that opened the field now covers the passwordless, cross-device world in "Anchors of Trust: A Usability Study on User Awareness, Consent, and Control in Cross-Device Authentication." Perhaps most telling of where things are headed, "Know Me by My Pulse" (NDSS 2026) pushes toward continuous, always-on authentication from wrist-worn PPG sensors, signaling a move beyond the one-time login prompt toward identity that is verified continuously in the background.
